articles.title: 5 JavaScript Mistakes I Made as a Beginner (and How to Fix them)
articles.excerpt: When I started learning JavaScript, I broke things constantly. Looking back, the same five mistakes caused most of my headaches. Here they are, with the fixes. Using var everywhere. I didn't understan…
articles.body: When I started learning JavaScript, I broke things constantly. Looking back, the same five mistakes caused most of my headaches. Here they are, with the fixes. Using var everywhere. I didn't understand that var is function-scoped, so variables leaked out of loops and blocks and caused strange bugs. Fix: use let for values that change and const for everything else. Confusing == with ===. Loose equality converts types silently, so "5" == 5 returned true. Fix: default to strict equality (===) and compare values of the same type. Losing track of this. Inside regular functions, this changed depending on how the function was called, and my callbacks broke. Fix: use arrow functions for callbacks, which inherit this from the surrounding code. Messy event listeners.
articles.author: ofodilechiemerie78-glitch

articles.title: Why Disabling Downloads Does Not Revoke a Signed URL
articles.excerpt: A photographer disables downloads for a private client gallery. The download button disappears immediately. An API test confirms that new download requests return 403. Then someone pastes a previously…
articles.body: A photographer disables downloads for a private client gallery. The download button disappears immediately. An API test confirms that new download requests return 403 . Then someone pastes a previously generated file URL into another browser. The original image still downloads. Nothing is necessarily broken in the storage service. The application changed its permissions, but an earlier request had already produced a separate credential: a signed URL. This is a common trap when building private media delivery. The permission check and the actual file transfer happen in different systems, at different times. A signed URL is a temporary credential Consider this request flow: Browser → Application: May I download asset 42?
articles.author: Edmond Rätzel

articles.title: Month-end reconciliation took me a full afternoon until I pasted two lists
articles.excerpt: Every month I closed the books by opening my invoice list and my Stripe export in two windows and eyeballing rows against each other. It took an afternoon, I still found mismatches the next day, and "…
articles.body: Every month I closed the books by opening my invoice list and my Stripe export in two windows and eyeballing rows against each other. It took an afternoon, I still found mismatches the next day, and "partially paid" was a special kind of pain because it lived only in my head. ReconcileIO is the tool I built to collapse that afternoon. You paste your invoice list and your payment or Stripe export, and it returns a matched table: paid, partial, or unpaid, with no spreadsheet in between. The matching is the boring part a computer should do, and now it does. Why eyeballing two lists fails Humans are bad at comparing long lists row by row, especially when the values don't line up exactly.
articles.author: LXSAIHUB

articles.title: Two languages, one catalog: the hreflang mistakes we made on a Hebrew/English store
articles.excerpt: Our store, RAMO, sells hardware and plumbing supplies in Israel. Most customers shop in Hebrew, but a real share of people search in English, so every product, category and article exists twice: once…
articles.body: Our store, RAMO, sells hardware and plumbing supplies in Israel. Most customers shop in Hebrew, but a real share of people search in English, so every product, category and article exists twice: once under /he/ and once under /en/ . On paper that's a solved problem. You add hreflang tags, Google figures out which version to show, done. In practice we got it wrong in a few small ways, and each one quietly made Search Console reports harder to trust. Here's what we tripped over. 1. Tags that pointed to pages that didn't exist The first version generated alternates by swapping the locale in the path: const alternates = { languages : { he : `https://www.ramo.co.il/he${path}` , en : `https://www.ramo.co.il/en${path}` , } , } ; Looks fine. The catch: not everything is translated.

I tested every feature below on Python 3.15.2 , and the outputs are real. Video version (3 minutes): 1. lazy import : load modules only when you use them lazy import json import sys print ( "json" in sys . modules ) # False: not loaded yet json . dumps ( { "ok" : True } ) # first use → loads now print ( "json" in sys . modules ) # True lazy import json doesn't load the module yet. The moment you actually use json , it loads. You keep normal-looking imports at the top of the file, but you only pay for the ones you use. lazy from decimal import Decimal works too. Does it matter?

articles.title: Why 'is' Lies to You in Python: 256 is 256, but 257 isn't (and 3.15 Changed It)
articles.excerpt: In Python 3.9, 256 is 256 is True, but 257 is 257 is False. And in Python 3.15, the answer changed. Here's why, and the real bug it causes. Video version: The weird part Python 3.9, typed line by line…
articles.body: In Python 3.9, 256 is 256 is True , but 257 is 257 is False . And in Python 3.15, the answer changed . Here's why, and the real bug it causes. Video version: The weird part Python 3.9, typed line by line in the REPL: >>> a = 256 >>> b = 256 >>> a is b True >>> x = 257 >>> y = 257 >>> x is y False # 🤯 >>> x == y True Same numbers, different answers. == compares values, is compares identity a == b asks: do they have the same value? a is b asks: are they the same object in memory?
articles.author: Muiduzzaman Lipu

articles.title: What to time when benchmarking in-browser inference, after WebGPU returned empty masks
articles.excerpt: Does WebGPU beat WASM for in-browser video matting? The first results table in this test said yes, 35.0 ms per 1280×720 frame on WebGPU against 87.2 ms on WASM with 4 threads. The output check said ot…
articles.body: Does WebGPU beat WASM for in-browser video matting? The first results table in this test said yes, 35.0 ms per 1280×720 frame on WebGPU against 87.2 ms on WASM with 4 threads. The output check said otherwise. By frame 13 the WebGPU alpha mask had 0.00% foreground pixels, while WASM had 5.03%, and nothing threw or warned. The benchmark had timed a backend that quickly computed an empty mask, hence a checklist instead of a speed chart. The model is the 7.5 MB RVM MobileNetV3 FP16 file that the video matting tool on ImgIng https://imging.ai/ loads for its lightest tier, run through ONNX Runtime Web 1.27.0 in desktop Chromium on an Apple M4 Mac.

articles.body: SpaceX is one big step closer to the 15th test flight of its Starship megarocket. The company announced today (Nov. 10) that it had moved its latest Starship first stage, known as Super Heavy Booster 22, to the launch mount at its Starbase facility in South Texas ahead of Flight 15, which is scheduled to lift off this Friday (Nov. 13). During the upcoming launch test, SpaceX plans to catch both Booster 22 and Starship's Ship upper stage with its launch tower's "chopstick" arms in a double landing catch — something the private spaceflight company has never tried before. articles.body: In any respectable audiobook project, finding the names of Andy Weir ("The Martian," "Project Hail Mary") and Benjamin Percy ("The Ninth Metal," "Wolverine") attached would elicit intense fan interest, but add the superstar vocal talents of Anthony Mackie ("Avengers: Infinity War," "Avengers: Doomsday"), Ariana DeBose ("West Side Story"), and John Leguizamo ("Ice Age"), and it catapults this sonic odyssey into the stratosphere. Such is the case with " Exoplanet ," Audible Original’s new 7-episode science fiction audio drama executive produced by Weir and penned by Percy. Its planet-hopping space disaster narrative sees the crew of the starship Wild Blue Yonder hit a quantum anomaly, forcing their ship to crash-land onto a deadly exoplanet.

articles.title: Microsoft Fixes Nearly 1,100 Security Vulnerabilities
articles.excerpt: Microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software. This month's Patch Tuesday ad…
articles.body: Microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software. This month’s Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws — including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook — and comes amid important security updates from other software makers, including Adobe , Apple , Google and Mozilla . Image: Shutterstock.com. Diorama by @zepp1969. November’s patch release from Redmond tackles 1,093 vulnerabilities, fixing 63 “critical” flaws that can be exploited to seize control over a Windows system with little or no help from users. Nearly half of those critical bugs are remote code execution vulnerabilities.
articles.author: BrianKrebs

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 10, 2013: Europe's GOCE satellite, the 'Ferrari of space,' fell out of orbit after mapping Earth's gravity field
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 10, 2013, Europe's GOCE satellite fell to Earth after four years in orbit mapping the planet's gravitational field. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 10, 2013, Europe's GOCE satellite fell to Earth after four years in orbit mapping the planet's gravitational field. GOCE, its name was short for Gravity field and steady-state Ocean Circulation Explorer, launched in 2009 on a mission to map Earth's gravity like never before. But despite that successful mission, it was doomed in 2013 when it ran out of fuel . At the time, controllers weren't sure where GOCE would fall back to Earth . Some people worried that it might crash into a populated area. However, the small spacecraft broke up in the atmosphere and didn't cause any property damage. It disintegrated about 50 miles above the Falkland Islands in the South Atlantic Ocean. The European Space Agency called the mission a success. GOCE lasted far longer than expected.
articles.author: Hanneke Weitering

articles.title: Grok Build coding agent leaks oodles of confidential info, some belonging to SpaceXSI
articles.excerpt: Researcher finds 35,000 Grok Build apps wide open to anyone who looked for them.
articles.body: Grok Build, the vibe-coding agent from SpaceXSI, is leaking data—some of it proprietary business information and other sensitive secrets—from thousands of its users, including the very same Elon Musk-owned company that offers the platform, new research shows. The information is revealed through links allowing Grok Build users to share their apps with others. Grok takes steps to randomize the URLs so only people who know the exact URL can access the data stored there. A design decision by developers of the platform, however, completely torpedoes that objective and makes it possible for anyone to enumerate thousands of live Grok Build projects. Except in rare cases, clicking those links opens the app and reveals all data associated with it.
